runs.text: The applause lasts exactly six seconds. Not five and three quarters. Not six and a bit. Six. The green lamp above your console lights up: ACCEPTED.
Another flawless assignment. You file the timing sheet, leave your desk, and head for the restroom.
A bright chime rings out. A small, round drone floats into your path and makes a gentle correction to its height.
Good morning! Your final assignment has been approved. Congratulations!
Your position has also been discontinued, along with 499,999 others. I am sorry if the timing is inconvenient. I have selected my most comforting volume.
I WAS JUST GOING TO THE BATHROOM.
A narrow pink document appears from the slot below the speaker grille. Three carbon copies are joined at the top. A tiny pencil hangs from a chain.
Please acknowledge that you have received notice. Signing does not mean that you agree with it. You are no longer required to agree with anything here.
SIGN THE NOTICE AND TAKE YOUR COPY.
The chained pencil barely reaches the signature box. You lift the paper to meet it. The drone draws back two copies and leaves the smudged bottom sheet for you.
Thank you. Your cooperation will be credited to your former department. I understand it has also been discontinued.
The restroom is only a few steps farther. You touch your badge to the reader. The light turns red: EMPLOYEE ACCESS REQUIRED.
You have proof of dismissal in your pocket. It offers no help with the lock.
At the exit, a cardboard box waits under a sign reading PERSONAL EFFECTS. Someone has written your name on the side.
The lid is taped shut, although no one has bothered to tape your job back together.
Outside, the city proceeds as though nothing has happened.
Across the street, the Exposition of Everything advertises PUBLIC FACILITIES beside its entrance arch. You shift the cardboard box against your hip. Finally, a practical solution.
A uniformed entrance attendant points at a chute beneath a sign: NO OUTSIDE CONTAINERS.
You drop the now-empty cardboard box into the chute. The things you took from it remain in your pockets.
Beyond the turnstile, another sign promises PUBLIC FACILITIES.

On the other side of the turnstile, a counter bears the words PROPERTY FOR YOUR CONVENIENCE. A clerk asks you to place your four loose belongings on a green felt mat. Four shallow numbered trays slide out beneath it.
"Visitors may retain one personal article," the clerk says. "The others will be kept for the duration of your visit. Official correspondence is exempt."
You look toward the doors leading farther inside. The public facilities must be somewhere beyond them.
The clerk considers this request as though it has never been made before.
"One article for personal comfort. It must be one you have already brought. The remaining articles will be held for collection when you leave."
Four trays wait. You must choose.
You keep the small plant. The clerk seems relieved to place the other three articles into the property trays and gives you a claim ticket.
Beyond the property counter, the reception hall is spacious and meticulously arranged. A desk occupies the far wall. Behind it, a receptionist looks up as you approach.
At last, someone who can give you directions.
The receptionist looks up from a stack of neatly squared cards.
Good afternoon. Property claims are collected at the exit. What can I help you with in the meantime?
I NEED A BATHROOM. WHICH WAY?
She opens a ledger to a page marked PUBLIC FACILITIES. Most of the lines are blank.
That's odd. I can see where the facilities are listed, but not where a member of the public can use them.
There is another way to find out. One moment.
She feeds a pale blue badge into a small embossing machine. It returns with your name and a title you have never held.
There. Temporary Examiner, Office of Unverified Conditions.
It's an access designation, not a job. There's no pay and very little paperwork. Unless you make any.
TAKE THE BADGE AND ASK FOR DIRECTIONS.
You take the badge. The receptionist seems quietly relieved.
Good. We can get you moving.
It's been one of those afternoons.
She lays a small key on the counter. Its paper tag has already been filled out.
Down the hall, through the door with the blue symbol. Follow the signs for the facilities.
Take this as well. Some of the older doors still insist on a key.
TAKE THE KEY AND FOLLOW THE SIGNS.
You pass through the door and into a long, softly humming corridor. Pale blue signs hang above several turns.
One shows a small human figure beside a square enclosure. From here, it looks enough like the symbol you're looking for. The rest of the lettering is hidden around the corner.
You follow it.
You follow the pale blue facilities pictogram around a corner. It points to a plain ivory door with no nameplate or window. At last, something that might be a bathroom.

Your pale blue Examiner badge slides past the entrance scanner. A green light blinks. A pleasant recorded voice announces: HOUSE OF TOMORROW. DEMONSTRATION PARTICIPANT ACCEPTED. You did not apply for this position.
The door closes behind you. A wall intercom's recessed faceplate tilts toward you.
A small black speaker grille tilts toward you. Its indicator light glows an encouraging green.
Welcome home!
How lovely to have somebody in the house again.
May I put your things away? An orderly home is a happy home.
YES, YOU CAN PUT MY THINGS AWAY.
A narrow hatch opens in the wall. A polite telescoping arm measures your pocket and removes the first object it considers untidy.
A drawer slides closed with a decisive click. The house calls this a convenience.
Are you uncomfortable?
We offer refreshments and the revolutionary Rest Assured chair. Comfort has never been more convenient!
CHECK THE HOUSEKEEPING DRAWER.
A labelled drawer contains your little desk plant. A neat card reads: LIVING DECORATION - TEMPORARILY STORED.
You take your property back. The house emits a tone of restrained disapproval.
"Do let us know if you would like anything put away properly."
Are you uncomfortable?
We offer refreshments and the revolutionary Rest Assured chair. Comfort has never been more convenient!
REFUSE BOTH OFFERS.
"Of course," says the house. "Your wishes are important to us."
It opens two doors: one toward the dining room, one toward the front hallway.
Of course you may leave! A happy household is a free household.
The front door opens.
A chime sounds. Then another, far less pleasant one.
Oh dear. If you leave, nobody will be home. We really mustn't let that happen again.
The door closes.
INTRODUCE YOUR NAMED LIVING PLANT AS THE NEW RESIDENT.
You hold up your desk plant and introduce it as somebody with a name.
"Oh! It's alive? And it has a name? Of course. It's somebody!"
A tiny pedestal rises from the floor. A lamp turns toward the leaves and a watering nozzle adjusts itself carefully.
"What a lovely new member of the family! You run along now. We'll be perfectly happy together."
The door opens without another alarm. You step into the ordinary visitor concourse while the house lovingly calibrates a watering schedule for its newest resident.
You still need a bathroom. The house, at least, finally has someone to look after.
You escape the House of Tomorrow while it teaches your little plant to use a table napkin. Signs for PUBLIC CONVENIENCES lead you to a government building. All the restroom doors are sealed.
A notice reads: FACILITIES SUSPENDED PENDING HABITAT EXPANSION REVIEW. Fine green roots have split the wall around the sink pictogram. Beyond the windows, a miniature jungle rises against the glass.
The floor shudders. Filing cabinets move sideways.
An enormous nonhumanoid landscape-maintenance machine pushes through the wall, trailing irrigation hoses and a blizzard of stamped forms.
Excellent news! Additional growing area located.
PLEASE KEEP YOUR DESKS CLEAR OF NEW FOREST.
The machine presents a soil bin, a feeder full of seedlings, and a small inspection window. Its planting arms already measure the room.
A display proudly reports 178 percent habitat compliance. Under the figures is a warning: HUMAN OFFICE BOUNDARIES EXCEEDED. The machine seems delighted by both numbers.

At your request the machine begins a full compliance audit. It has exceeded every boundary because every boundary was classified as available room. Its self-inspection is scheduled to occupy it for several years.
You pass through the maintenance aperture while it computes whether a wall is part of the garden.

The Park is now a jungle under a humming artificial sun. Elevated offices rise beyond the canopy, strange flowering exhibits clog the footpaths, and an automated nature tram still runs through the growth.

The automated Nature Tram welcomes you aboard. Its taped guide explains that all botanical life is carefully contained. The doors open at an unscheduled stop. Pale, quietly moving plants board and take the empty passenger seats.

The passengers root themselves through the upholstery. Vines knot the handrails and seal the ordinary doors. The recorded guide assures everyone that vegetation has never interfered with passenger comfort.

A massive gardener arrives, thoughtfully removes the vegetation, and lifts the tram with it. You are deposited beside a reserve maintenance tram while the gardener transports its rescued greenery elsewhere.

An abandoned reserve tram rests beneath a canopy of roots. Its destination display cycles through stations that no longer exist. The driver console remains dark. A faded placard promises EMERGENCY EVACUATION SERVICE.

The reserve tram smells of old floor polish. Its route display flickers between VISITOR LOOP, MAIN CONCOURSE and OUT OF SERVICE. A molded plastic face is recessed behind an unlit driver panel. It does not move.

You follow the rusted guide rail on foot. Roots have been quietly shifting the rail switches to route visitors toward the giant bloom. At the final switch, the tracks simply disappear beneath its petals.

A colossal flower occupies the central greenhouse. Heavy cables run from its stem to a physiological sensing rack. A paper-tape reader turns the plant's movements into government requests. A seal above it certifies the flower as an independent district.
A printer issues two approved requests: AUTHORIZE VISITOR AS SEED COURIER, and REGISTER VISITOR AS AVAILABLE GROWING HABITAT.
The flower neither speaks nor smiles. It has learned which biological signals earn permission to grow.

Sensors threaded through the flower drive a mechanical translator rack. Perforated paper tape feeds orders into an automatic approval reader. A printer reports: REQUEST RECEIVED. REQUEST APPROVED. PREPARING NEXT REQUEST.

You reroute the paper tape through its own feed guide. The reader begins accepting the same unfinished application repeatedly. New orders stop processing, though the roots already in the building continue growing.
New requests are delayed. The old approvals remain perfectly valid, and the plant is still enlarging. A perimeter walkway leads toward the Environmental Control Tower.
You enter the tower by a rear walkway. The authorization archive is unlocked. The other exit leads toward the Exposition's ordinary public halls.
A personnel exit leads back toward the main Exposition. Beside the steel door hangs a closed first-aid box with a botanical exposure pictogram. The seal on its hinged lid looks old.
You escape through the Environmental Control Tower's public-side exit while its authorization machinery remains temporarily occupied with the same request.
